nameStory: This hawk is named after William Swainson, a British naturalist who studied and collected birds in the early 1800s. It's also called the "grasshopper hawk" or "locust hawk" because of its incredible appetite for these crunchy insects - it will gobble them up whenever they're available!
description: Swainson's Hawk is a large bird of prey that's built for soaring over open grasslands and prairies. These impressive raptors are long-distance travelers, spending their summers breeding in western North America and flying all the way to Argentina for winter - one of the longest migrations of any hawk. They're medium to large-sized hawks with broad wings perfect for riding thermals, and they have a particular fondness for grasshoppers and locusts.

idTips.label: Wing shape in flight
idTips.description: Long, broad wings held in a slight V-shape when soaring, with pointed wingtips that often show distinct 'fingers' of separated feathers

idTips.label: Chest banding
idTips.description: Adults typically show a distinctive dark chest band across the upper breast, contrasting with lighter belly and throat

idTips.label: Tail pattern
idTips.description: Gray-brown tail with multiple thin dark bands and a broader dark band near the tip

idTips.label: Head coloring
idTips.description: Light-colored head and face, often appearing almost white from a distance, with dark eyes

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Soars in large circles over open areas, often flying in groups during migration, with steady wingbeats when flapping

habitat: In New England, Swainson's Hawks are extremely rare visitors, typically seen only during migration in open agricultural areas, large fields, and grasslands. They prefer wide-open spaces similar to their western prairie breeding grounds, so look for them over farmland, meadows, and airports during fall migration.

seasonality.spring: Very rarely seen in New England during spring migration, typically in May if at all. Any sightings would be of birds passing through on their way to western breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during breeding season, as they nest in western prairies and grasslands far from our region.
seasonality.fall: Most likely time to spot one in New England, usually September through October during their epic migration to Argentina. Look for them soaring over open fields.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England in winter - they're spending this season thousands of miles south in the grasslands of Argentina.

funFact: Swainson's Hawks make one of the most incredible migrations in the bird world - they fly roughly 14,000 miles roundtrip from their breeding grounds in western North America all the way to Argentina, often traveling in flocks of hundreds or even thousands of birds!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Red-tailed Hawks, but Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings, a distinctive dark chest band (Red-tails have belly bands), and lighter heads. Memory trick: Swainson's are 'long and lean' compared to the chunkier Red-tailed Hawks.
contextualKnowledge: With only 33 recorded observations in all of New England, seeing a Swainson's Hawk here is truly exceptional and would be considered a rare vagrant - a bird far outside its normal range. Most New England birders go their entire lives without seeing one locally.
compareHints: Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring. Unlike Broad-winged Hawks which also migrate long distances, Swainson's are much larger and lack the distinctive white tail bands. They're more slender overall than the stocky Rough-legged Hawks that visit in winter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas.
Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern.
Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory.
Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic.
Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build.
